transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, um... I guess I came in because I just can’t shake this... this incredibly heavy, hopeless feeling. It’s just always there right now, pressing down on me. 

You see, my whole career is about building things that last—making sure the foundation is solid, calculating load-bearing capacities, all of that. And after my divorce... well, that was a whole ordeal, but after it was finalized, I really thought I had rebuilt my life. I put so much effort into making sure every piece was secure, getting everything back on track, laying down new groundwork. 

But now... I don't even know how to explain it, it just feels like everything I built after the divorce has completely collapsed. Just caved in on itself. And I’m just sitting under it. Like I'm literally trapped under the rubble of my own life, and the weight of it is just so overwhelming. I keep going over it in my head, trying to figure out why it fell apart, but I just feel this crushing hopelessness instead. I can't lift it. I can't move. I'm just stuck sitting under it all, and it's... it's just so heavy.
How long have you been feeling this heavy, hopeless feeling?

Well, it’s... it’s been about a month now. A whole month of just waking up every single day and feeling like there’s a concrete slab resting on my chest before I even open my eyes. I can actually trace it back, you know, to right around the time the financial mess from the divorce really started hitting me. Because, see, when the divorce was finalized, I thought the worst was over. I thought, okay, the emotional part is done, the legal part is done, now I just have to reconstruct. 

But then the financial reality set in. The lawyer fees, dividing the assets, realizing that the savings I had carefully calculated for my future—for a down payment on a new place—were just gone. Evaporated. And I’m someone who plans for everything. I run contingencies at work all day long, I account for stress and strain and unexpected variables, but I just... I didn't account for how completely decimated my finances would be. 

So it started then, about four weeks ago, right when I got this one particular statement from the bank that just laid it all out in black and white. And ever since that day, this dark cloud just rolled in and parked itself right over me. It hasn't lifted for a single second since. It’s just this constant, suffocating presence, day in and day out, for an entire month now. I keep trying to logically work my way out of it, like a problem to solve, but I just can't.
Do you find yourself enjoying things you used to like before this heavy feeling started?

No. No, I don't. And that's... that's actually one of the things that scares me the most, honestly. Because, you know, I used to love my work. I genuinely did. There was this deep satisfaction in looking at a set of blueprints, spotting a potential structural flaw, and figuring out exactly how to reinforce it before a single drop of concrete was poured. I used to get this rush from solving those problems, from knowing I was making something safe and strong. 

But now? Now I look at those same plans and I feel absolutely nothing. It’s just lines on paper. The numbers don't mean anything to me anymore. And it's not just work, either. I used to go hiking every weekend. I loved being out in nature, away from the city, just feeling the ground under my boots and breathing the fresh air. I had this whole routine—I'd pack my gear on Friday night, wake up at dawn on Saturday, and just go. It was my way of resetting. 

But since this... this heavy feeling started, I haven't even looked at my hiking boots. They're just sitting by the door, gathering dust. The thought of packing my bag, driving out to the trailhead, even just getting out of bed to do it... it just seems completely impossible. It’s like the color has been drained out of everything. Even the food I used to love—I used to cook these elaborate meals on Sundays, trying out new recipes, but now everything just tastes like ash. I just eat toast because it's easy and I don't have to think about it. It’s like the part of my brain that registers pleasure or interest has just been completely shut off, and I don't know how to turn it back on. I try to force myself, I really do. I tell myself, "Just go for a short walk, just look at one set of plans," but the energy just isn't there. It's just this massive, gaping void where my life used to be.
Have you had any thoughts about harming yourself since this heavy feeling started?

Well... yes. I... I have. And I hate admitting it, I really do, because it feels like just another structural failure on my part, you know? Like I couldn't bear the load. But... it started as just this passive thought. I’d be lying in bed, staring at the ceiling, feeling that concrete slab on my chest, and I’d just think... wouldn’t it be so much easier if I just didn’t wake up? If I could just go to sleep and the weight would be gone, and I wouldn't have to figure out how to rebuild everything from scratch again. 

I wasn't planning anything at first, it was just... an escape hatch in my mind. A way out of the pressure. But then, over the last week or so, the thoughts started getting louder. More persistent. I'd be driving over a bridge—one I actually helped inspect a few years ago, ironically enough—and I'd catch myself looking at the guardrail and calculating the drop. Or I'd be standing in my kitchen, looking at my medication bottles, and just... wondering. 

And then a few nights ago, it got really bad. I was sitting on my living room floor, surrounded by all these financial documents that I was trying to organize, and the hopelessness just hit me so hard I couldn't breathe. The thoughts got so intense, so specific, that I actually terrified myself. I realized I was dangerously close to crossing a line from just wanting the pain to stop to actually making it stop. It was like watching a building sway in the wind and knowing it was about to snap. 

I got so scared of what I might do that I grabbed my phone and called the employee assistance program through my work. I just dialed the number because it was the only lifeline I could think of in that exact second. I talked to someone there for a long time, and they told me I needed to come in and see a professional immediately. So... that's why I'm here. Because I'm scared of my own brain right now, and I don't trust myself alone with these thoughts anymore. They're just too heavy to carry by myself.
Have you noticed any changes in your energy levels or how you're moving, like feeling restless or slowed down?

Well, honestly, it's... it's like I'm moving through molasses. Or, no, it's more like... you know when you're pouring a foundation and the concrete is just too wet, too heavy, and you're trying to drag the screed board across it to level it out? That's what my body feels like right now. Every single movement is just this immense, dragging effort. 

Getting through a normal workday right now... it's agonizing. I used to be the first one in the office, energized, ready to tackle the site reports. Now, just the act of sitting at my desk and trying to open my laptop feels like I'm trying to lift a steel beam with my bare hands. I just stare at the screen and think about how much energy it's going to take to type out a single email, and I just... I don't have it. I don't have the energy. 

And it's not just work. It's everything. The basic, fundamental things that a person is supposed to just do without thinking. Like taking a shower. I used to take a shower every morning, right after my run, clockwork. Now, I stand in the bathroom and look at the showerhead, and the thought of undressing, turning on the water, washing my hair, drying off... it's exhausting just conceptualizing it. It takes more energy than I seem to have in my entire body. I've gone three days without showering this week, which is so unlike me, I'm usually so meticulous about hygiene, especially working around construction sites where you get dust on everything. 

But I just feel so incredibly slowed down. My limbs feel heavy, my thoughts feel heavy. If the phone rings, it takes me three rings just to coordinate my hand to pick it up. I'm not restless at all, I'm just... anchored to the floor. It's like gravity has multiplied by ten just for me, and I'm using every ounce of strength I have just to remain upright, let alone actually move forward.
Have you lost a significant amount of weight since this heavy feeling started?

I don't... I don't really know, to be honest. I haven't stepped on a scale in weeks. I mean, I mentioned earlier that I'm basically just eating toast, right? So you would think that living off plain bread would make me drop a lot of weight, but I haven't really noticed a huge difference. 

Maybe my clothes are a little looser? It's hard to tell because I've just been wearing the same two pairs of fleece sweatpants for... well, for a while now. They have drawstrings, so they just kind of adjust to whatever, you don't really notice if your waistline changes. I used to wear these really tailored, heavy-duty canvas work pants to the job sites—Carhartts, mostly, because they hold up against the rebar and the concrete dust—and they were always pretty fitted. If I put those on, I could probably tell you if I lost weight. But I haven't put those on since this heavy feeling started. I just can't bring myself to put on real clothes with buttons and zippers. 

And I used to be so on top of tracking my weight, too. I had this Bluetooth scale that synced directly to an app on my phone, tracking my BMI and my muscle mass and all these metrics. I treated it like a structural health report for my own body, checking the tolerances and making sure everything was in alignment. I loved having that data. But now... that scale is just sitting on the bathroom floor right next to the shower I'm not taking. I think the battery might even be dead by now. I just look at it and feel absolutely nothing. 

So, I might have lost a few pounds just from skipping meals and not having any interest in food, but nothing significant that I'm actually aware of. I just don't have the energy to gather that data or care what the number is anymore.
Do you feel guilty about anything in particular since this heavy feeling started?

Guilty... God, yes. It's... it's honestly all I can think about when I'm not just staring at the wall. It’s like this constant, running loop in my head, just broadcasting all my failures on a giant screen. I just... I look at my life right now, and I keep telling myself I’m a terrible engineer, a failed wife, and just... a massive, heavy burden on everyone around me. 

My husband, he... he tries to be patient, he really does, but I see him looking at me sitting there in those same sweatpants, and the guilt just eats me alive. I’m supposed to be his partner, you know? We’re supposed to be building a life together, laying down a solid foundation for our future, and instead, I’m just this... this sinkhole in the middle of our living room. I tell myself I'm a failed wife because I can't even contribute the bare minimum anymore. I'm just a burden he has to drag around on top of all his own responsibilities. 

And then my brain pivots to work, and it's just as bad, if not worse. I keep telling myself I'm a terrible engineer. And it’s not just a general feeling—my mind actually goes digging for the evidence to support it. I will literally lie there and replay every single missed calculation I’ve ever made. Like, the other night, I spent hours agonizing over a load-bearing calculation for a retaining wall from three years ago. Three years! It was caught in the peer review phase, it never even made it to the site, no one was ever in danger, but right now? Right now, my brain treats it like this unforgivable crime. 

Or I'll obsess over a tense email I sent to a concrete supplier last month. I’ll replay the exact phrasing of that email over and over and over again in my head, analyzing every single word, convincing myself I was completely toxic and out of line. 

It's like I'm compiling this massive, undeniable structural report on my own flaws. Every missed calculation, every tense email, every day I can't get off the floor for my husband... I just use it all as definitive proof that I ruin things. I ruin projects, I ruin my marriage, I ruin everything I touch. The guilt is just... it's suffocating. It's just as heavy as that physical weight I told you about. You can't just put it down or walk away from it. It just stays there, crushing you, telling you that you're entirely at fault for all of it.
Have you experienced any thoughts or beliefs that seem unreal or detached from reality since this heavy feeling started?

Unreal? Like... like imagining things, or believing things that aren't actually happening? No, no, I haven't had anything like that. I mean, my whole life, my entire career as an engineer, it’s all built on reality, right? On physics. On tangible, measurable facts. Gravity, load distribution, tensile strength, material tolerances... you can't just detach from those things, or the whole structure collapses. You have to live in reality. 

So, my thoughts right now... they aren't detached from reality at all. If anything, I feel like I'm hyper-focused on reality, just... the absolute bleakest, worst parts of it. Like I was just saying about the guilt, when I'm lying on the floor obsessing over that retaining wall calculation, that was a real project. That was a real mistake I made. I'm not fabricating it. The tense email to the concrete supplier, that was a real email that I actually typed and sent from my own outbox. I'm not imagining these events. 

I know sometimes people think weird things when they get really, really down, like... I don't know, thinking the television is sending them messages or that they're secretly someone else, but my brain doesn't do that. I don't have any bizarre theories about the world or anything like that. I just have this crushing, undeniable awareness of my own failures. And it feels very, very real. Honestly, it feels too real. 

My husband actually tried to tell me I was being irrational the other day when I couldn't stop crying about a site survey I did back in 2019, and I got so frustrated because I had to explain to him that it's not irrational to look at the data. The data says I made an error. The data says I'm flawed. It's just the facts of my incompetence catching up to me, plain as day. So no, I'm not detached from reality. I'm just... I'm just completely buried under the weight of it, and I can't get out.
Have you been feeling restless or fidgety since this heavy feeling started?

Restless? No, not really. I mean, I don't feel like I have the energy to be restless, if that makes sense. Like I said before, it's more like this massive, crushing weight just pressing down on me, pinning me to the floor. If anything, I feel the exact opposite of restless. I feel completely immobilized. 

I remember when I used to get restless, though. Like, back when I was working on that big bridge project downtown, the suspension one over the river. We had these insane deadlines, and I would be up at 2:00 AM, pacing around my home office, tapping my pen on the blueprints, just buzzing with this nervous energy because I needed to double-check the wind load calculations for the hundredth time. I couldn't sit still. My leg would be bouncing under the desk, and I’d be constantly getting up to refill my coffee or adjust the thermostat. That was restlessness. That was this internal motor just running too hot, you know? 

But now? Now the motor is completely flooded. It won't even turn over. I just lie there in those same fleece sweatpants, staring at the ceiling, and my body feels like it's made of lead. I don't have the urge to pace, I don't bounce my leg, I don't even really shift positions that much. My husband came in the other day after being gone for hours—he had to run to the hardware store because the handle on the guest bathroom toilet broke, and then he stopped at the grocery store to get more of that bread I’ve been eating—and he said I was in the exact same spot, in the exact same position, as when he left. I hadn't moved a muscle. 

It's almost like the gravity in my specific location has been dialed up by a factor of ten. You can't be fidgety when you feel like you're fighting just to lift your arm, you know? It takes so much effort just to sit up, let alone pace around or fidget. So, no, I wouldn't say I'm restless at all. I'm just... stuck. Completely and utterly stuck in place.
Do you find it difficult to initiate or complete everyday tasks due to feeling slowed down?

Difficult? Oh, God, difficult doesn't even begin to cover it. It's... it's nearly impossible. Every single thing I try to do, every tiny, mundane task that used to just be automatic, it's like I have to summit a mountain just to get it done. 

It’s the fatigue, you know? It’s just this bone-deep, overwhelming exhaustion that never, ever lifts, no matter how long I lie on that floor. Just... getting through a normal workday right now... I mean, when I actually manage to log on, which is rare these days... it feels exactly like dragging wet concrete. Have you ever tried to move wet concrete? It’s dense, it’s heavy, it fights you every single inch of the way, and that’s what my brain and my body feel like right now. I’ll sit down at my desk—well, I’ll try to sit at my desk, if I make it that far—and just the thought of opening my laptop... just reaching out, lifting the lid, and waiting for the screen to wake up... it takes more energy than I seem to have. 

And it’s not just work. It’s the everyday stuff, the things that shouldn't even register as tasks. Like taking a shower. I’ll lie there, and I’ll tell myself, 'Okay, you need to get up. You need to walk to the bathroom, turn on the water, and get in.' And I will break it down into these microscopic steps, like a project schedule, you know? Step one: sit up. Step two: put feet on floor. Step three: stand. But I get stuck on step one. The energy required to just shift my center of gravity and sit up feels so monumental that I just... I can't. 

My husband will come in and gently suggest I take a shower, and I want to, I really do, because I know I probably smell and my hair is a greasy mess, but the physical toll of just standing under the water... it’s like asking me to run a marathon. It’s not just feeling slowed down, it’s like my battery is completely dead, and no amount of rest recharges it. I just don't have the fuel to initiate anything, let alone complete it. Everything just feels so incredibly hard and heavy.
Have you thought about or planned a specific way to harm yourself?

A specific way? Um... no. No, not a specific plan. Like, I haven't worked out the logistics or the... the mechanics of it, if that's what you mean. I honestly don't have the energy to plan a grocery list right now, let alone figure out a step-by-step procedure for... for harming myself. 

But... I have been having these thoughts. A lot. I’ve just been thinking that it would be so much easier if I didn’t wake up. 

It started out as just this vague wish, you know? Like when you're a kid and you wish for a snow day so you don't have to go to school and face a test you didn't study for. I would just lie there on the floor, or in bed when my husband finally coerces me to move there, and I’d think about how peaceful it would be if the system just... shut down. No more crushing guilt, no more trying to lift this wet concrete body, no more analyzing every single mistake I've ever made in my career. Just... off. I’d go to sleep and just fade out, and I wouldn't have to carry this weight anymore. 

But then... a few days ago, it stopped being just a passing wish. The thoughts got really, really intense. It wasn't just a quiet idea anymore, it was like this loud, overwhelming conviction that ceasing to exist was the only logical solution to stop the pain. And that... that really scared me. I've always been in control of my mind. I'm an engineer, I rely on my brain to be rational and objective, and suddenly my own brain is telling me that not waking up is the best possible outcome. 

It terrified me. It scared me so much that I actually managed to find my phone—it was buried under a pile of blankets somewhere—and I called the employee assistance program at my firm. I don't even really remember exactly what I said to the person on the line, I think I was just crying and trying to explain that I was terrified of my own thoughts. I just knew I needed to do something, reach out to someone, before the thoughts turned into something I couldn't take back. So, no, I don't have a specific plan to do anything, but the thoughts of just... not being here... they've been really hard to fight off.
Have you been feeling fidgety or having an inability to sit still since this heavy feeling started?

I... wait, didn't you just ask me that? Or something really similar? I'm sorry, my brain is just so foggy right now, but I feel like I just went over this a minute ago when I was talking about the bridge project and my husband going to the hardware store. 

But, um, just to be completely clear... no. No fidgeting. No inability to sit still. Like I was trying to explain before with the wet concrete analogy, it's really the exact opposite problem. It’s an inability to *stop* being still. 

You know how when you're just sitting in a chair, even if you're perfectly comfortable, your body naturally makes these tiny micro-adjustments? You cross your ankles, or you shift your weight, or you reach up to scratch your collarbone without even thinking about it. It's just a baseline level of human movement, this subconscious kinetic energy that everyone has. Well, I don't even have that right now. I don't make those micro-adjustments. I just lie there on the floor in my living room, completely static, for hours on end. 

It’s like the signal from my brain to my muscles just... isn't connecting. Or it’s connecting, but the physical resistance of my own body is just too high to overcome. My husband actually gets worried because he'll look over and I haven't even blinked or shifted a leg in forty-five minutes. So the idea of being fidgety or having nervous energy... it's just not physically possible for me right now. I don't have the fuel for it. I'm entirely anchored to whatever spot I happen to collapse in.
Have you experienced any hallucinations since this heavy feeling started?

Hallucinations? Like... seeing things or hearing voices that aren't there? Um, no. No, nothing like that at all. I mean, my mind is incredibly foggy, like I was saying, and everything feels so heavy and impossible, but my grip on reality... the physical reality of the room I'm in... that's all completely intact. 

Honestly, it's almost like... I don't know, sometimes I think it would be a distraction if my brain were making things up, because right now, the reality I'm staring at is just the baseboards of my living room for six hours straight. I just lie there on the floor and I see the dust bunnies accumulating, and I see this one specific scuff mark on the wall from when my husband and I moved the bookshelf last year... it's all very real, unfortunately. As an engineer, my brain is so rigidly trained to observe what's physically present in an environment, you know? Structural realities, material facts. I deal in what is actually there. And right now, what's there is just... this crushing, static weight. 

I don't hear any voices or anything either. I mean, unless you count my own internal monologue, which is just constantly, endlessly running this miserable loop about how useless I am, how I'm failing at my job, how I can't even stand up to wash my hair. But that's just me. That's my own voice in my own head, not an external hallucination. I don't see shadows moving or... or anything bizarre. Everything is actually painfully still. The room doesn't move, I don't move, time just sort of... stretches out and drags. So, no, my senses are processing everything exactly as they always have. They're just processing a really, really bleak existence right now.
Have you thought about how you would harm yourself if you decided to act on those thoughts?

Wait... I... I feel like we just talked about this, didn't we? I'm so sorry, my brain is just... it's like wading through molasses right now. I know I just answered a question about this, like, a few minutes ago. I was talking about the EAP hotline and... and the grocery lists...

But, just to reiterate, because I know you need to ask these things... no. No, I haven't thought about *how* I would do it. I haven't picked out a method or... or researched anything or gathered any... any materials. Like I said before, I don't have the energy to even think about the mechanics of something like that. As an engineer, if I were going to do a project, I'd have a timeline, a materials list, a risk assessment... I'd have a whole schematic drawn up. But I don't have any of that for this. I don't have the capacity for it. 

It's really just been those thoughts I mentioned earlier. The ones where I'm just lying there on the floor, staring at that scuff mark on the wall, and I just think... it would just be so much easier if I went to sleep and the system just never booted back up. If I just didn't wake up tomorrow. 

And like I said, it started out quiet, just this sort of exhausted wish to not have to deal with the crushing weight of my own body and my own failures anymore. But then it got so loud. It got so intense that it felt like the only logical conclusion to this... this endless loop of misery. And that's what terrified me. That's what made me dig my phone out from under the blankets and call the employee assistance program at work. Because I was so scared that my own brain, which is usually so rational, was telling me that ceasing to exist was a good idea. So, no, no plan on *how* to do it. Just... just the overwhelming thought that not being here would be a relief.
Are there any activities that you still find pleasure in or look forward to?

No. No, none at all. I mean... I used to love things. I used to be a person who looked forward to weekends. My husband and I, we used to do these elaborate Sunday morning breakfasts. He'd make the coffee, and I'd do this whole production with, like, sourdough pancakes or a frittata with whatever vegetables we had left over from the week. It was a whole routine, this little ritual we had to decompress after the work week. I used to genuinely look forward to that starting on, like, Thursday afternoon. I'd be sitting at my desk, looking at CAD drawings for a retaining wall, and I'd be thinking about what kind of cheese to put in the frittata. 

But now? Now the idea of Sunday morning just fills me with this... this dread. Because Sunday morning means I have to get out of bed, and I have to pretend to be a functional human being, and I have to look at my husband and know that I'm dragging him down into this swamp with me. I don't want to make pancakes. I don't even want to eat them. Food tastes like ash. It's just chewing and swallowing, just mechanical input. There's no joy in it.

And my work... I used to really get a deep sense of satisfaction out of my job. I'm a civil engineer, and there's something so inherently grounding about building infrastructure. You take a problem, you analyze the soil, you calculate the load-bearing requirements, and you design a solution that is going to stand there for fifty years, keeping people safe, keeping water where it belongs, keeping roads stable. I used to love that moment when a project went from paper to reality. That feeling of, 'I designed this, and it works.' 

But now, I just look at my screen and it's just lines. It's just meaningless lines and numbers, and the responsibility of it is suffocating. I don't care if the bridge holds. I mean, I do care, obviously, I'm not a monster, but I don't *feel* the satisfaction of it. It's just another impossible task on a list of impossible tasks. 

I don't read anymore, I don't watch TV... even just putting on a movie feels like too much of a commitment. I don't want to follow a plot. I don't want to care about characters. I just want to lie on the floor and stare at the baseboards. It's like... you know when you unplug a lamp, and the light just instantly dies? That's what happened to my capacity for pleasure. The cord got pulled, and there's just no current flowing anymore. There's absolutely nothing I look forward to. Nothing.
Do you feel like you're a burden to your loved ones?

Oh, god, yes. Yes, constantly. I mean, I was just saying how I feel like I'm dragging my husband down into this swamp with me, and that's... that's exactly it. I am a complete burden. I just look at him trying to hold our whole lives together, trying to do the grocery shopping and keep the house running while I'm literally just a useless lump on the floor, and I just keep telling myself what a failed wife I am. I'm completely failing him. 

And it doesn't stop with him, it bleeds into everything. My brain just runs this relentless loop telling me I'm a terrible engineer, too. I'll lie there staring at the wall, and my mind just starts pulling up this... this mental filing cabinet of every mistake I've ever made. I will literally replay every single missed calculation from years ago, or... or I'll obsess over some slightly tense email I sent to a contractor about a grading issue back in 2021. I'll just analyze the wording of this one stupid email over and over, holding it up as like... absolute proof that I ruin things. 

It's like I'm compiling this massive, undeniable dossier of evidence against myself. Proof that I'm incompetent at my job, proof that I'm a drain on my marriage, proof that everything I touch just fails. I just sift through all these past interactions, these tiny little moments that probably nobody else even remembers, and to me, they are just glaring red flags that I am a terrible person and a massive burden to everyone who has the misfortune of relying on me. I just can't stop replaying it all. Every missed decimal point, every awkward conversation... it just plays on a loop to remind me how much I ruin absolutely everything.
Do you feel like your heavy feeling is getting worse over time?

Worse... I mean, I don't even know if 'worse' really captures it anymore, because that implies there's a bottom to it, you know? But yes... it's just this constant, crushing weight. That’s actually the whole reason I came in, why I finally had to reach out for help. I just... I absolutely cannot shake this heavy, completely hopeless feeling. It just sits on my chest all day and all night. 

It’s like... well, as an engineer, I think about structural integrity a lot, right? After my divorce, I had to completely rebuild my life from the ground up. I had to pour a new foundation, put up new supports, literally reconstruct my entire existence piece by piece just to get back to a place where I was functioning and stable. It took so much work, so much effort to build that new life. And now... it feels like every single thing I built after that divorce has just suffered a catastrophic structural collapse. It all just completely caved in on itself. 

And I’m just... I'm just sitting under it. I'm sitting under all the rubble of my own life, all the concrete and the debris, and it's just pressing down on me. I can't dig myself out. I don't even have the energy to try to move the pieces or assess the damage. I'm just trapped under the weight of it all, and yeah, the longer I sit under it, the heavier and more hopeless it feels.
Do you think your heavy feeling is interfering with your ability to function in daily life?

Interfering... yeah. Yeah, it’s completely derailed everything. I mean, I was telling you earlier about how much I used to care about my job and the infrastructure and the calculations, right? Well, it got to the point where I was actually making really questionable calls at work. Like, I was reviewing a grading plan for this new commercial development, and I just... I couldn't process the elevation data anymore. I was signing off on things that just didn't make logical sense, just staring at the screen and guessing because my brain was so bogged down in that swamp. 

And then in meetings... oh god, the meetings. We have these weekly coordination meetings with the architects and city planners, and I would just sit there and completely fall apart. I'd start crying over a minor timeline adjustment, or I'd just freeze up, completely blank, and not be able to answer basic questions about soil compaction that I've known the answers to for ten years. It was so humiliating. Finally, my supervisor had to pull me into his office and officially take me off all active project decisions. He had to physically remove my authority because I was messing up so badly and he could see I was just crumbling in real time. 

And then at home... I know I mentioned the Sunday breakfasts earlier, but it goes so far beyond just not cooking. I completely stopped keeping up with basic routines. Any routine, really. I'm talking about going four or five days without showering, wearing the same sweatpants until they literally smell, letting the mail pile up on the counter until it falls onto the floor and I just step over it... I couldn't even brush my teeth. The effort required to just lift a toothbrush to my mouth felt like trying to lift a steel I-beam. 

And it just... it kept piling up, the inability to do anything, until it got so dark. I don't know, sometimes I think it would be a distraction if my brain were making things up, because right now, the reality I'm staring at is just the baseboards of my living room for six hours straight. I just lie there on the floor and I see the dust bunnies accumulating, and I see this one specific scuff mark on the wall from when my husband and I moved the bookshelf last year... it's all very real, unfortunately. As an engineer, my brain is so rigidly trained to observe what's physically present in an environment, you know? Structural realities, material facts. I deal in what is actually there. And right now, what's there is just... this crushing, static weight. 

I don't hear any voices or anything either. I mean, unless you count my own internal monologue, which is just constantly, endlessly running this miserable loop about how useless I am, how I'm failing at my job, how I can't even stand up to wash my hair. But that's just me. That's my own voice in my own head, not an external hallucination. I don't see shadows moving or... or anything bizarre. Everything is actually painfully still. The room doesn't move, I don't move, time just sort of... stretches out and drags. So, no, my senses are processing everything exactly as they always have. They're just processing a really, really bleak existence right now.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of suicidal intent with a plan
doctor.question: Have you thought about how you would harm yourself if you decided to act on those thoughts?

target_item.name: Death_Suicide
target_item.manifestation: I’ve been thinking that it would be easier if I didn’t wake up, and the thoughts got intense enough that I scared myself and called the employee assistance program.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about suicidal plans or methods, which directly relates to the symptom of suicidal ideation.

patient.answer:
Wait... I... I feel like we just talked about this, didn't we? I'm so sorry, my brain is just... it's like wading through molasses right now. I know I just answered a question about this, like, a few minutes ago. I was talking about the EAP hotline and... and the grocery lists...

But, just to reiterate, because I know you need to ask these things... no. No, I haven't thought about *how* I would do it. I haven't picked out a method or... or researched anything or gathered any... any materials. Like I said before, I don't have the energy to even think about the mechanics of something like that. As an engineer, if I were going to do a project, I'd have a timeline, a materials list, a risk assessment... I'd have a whole schematic drawn up. But I don't have any of that for this. I don't have the capacity for it. 

It's really just been those thoughts I mentioned earlier. The ones where I'm just lying there on the floor, staring at that scuff mark on the wall, and I just think... it would just be so much easier if I went to sleep and the system just never booted back up. If I just didn't wake up tomorrow. 

And like I said, it started out quiet, just this sort of exhausted wish to not have to deal with the crushing weight of my own body and my own failures anymore. But then it got so loud. It got so intense that it felt like the only logical conclusion to this... this endless loop of misery. And that's what terrified me. That's what made me dig my phone out from under the blankets and call the employee assistance program at work. Because I was so scared that my own brain, which is usually so rational, was telling me that ceasing to exist was a good idea. So, no, no plan on *how* to do it. Just... just the overwhelming thought that not being here would be a relief.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of anhedonia
doctor.question: Are there any activities that you still find pleasure in or look forward to?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about anhedonia (loss of interest or pleasure), which is not listed in the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No. No, none at all. I mean... I used to love things. I used to be a person who looked forward to weekends. My husband and I, we used to do these elaborate Sunday morning breakfasts. He'd make the coffee, and I'd do this whole production with, like, sourdough pancakes or a frittata with whatever vegetables we had left over from the week. It was a whole routine, this little ritual we had to decompress after the work week. I used to genuinely look forward to that starting on, like, Thursday afternoon. I'd be sitting at my desk, looking at CAD drawings for a retaining wall, and I'd be thinking about what kind of cheese to put in the frittata. 

But now? Now the idea of Sunday morning just fills me with this... this dread. Because Sunday morning means I have to get out of bed, and I have to pretend to be a functional human being, and I have to look at my husband and know that I'm dragging him down into this swamp with me. I don't want to make pancakes. I don't even want to eat them. Food tastes like ash. It's just chewing and swallowing, just mechanical input. There's no joy in it.

And my work... I used to really get a deep sense of satisfaction out of my job. I'm a civil engineer, and there's something so inherently grounding about building infrastructure. You take a problem, you analyze the soil, you calculate the load-bearing requirements, and you design a solution that is going to stand there for fifty years, keeping people safe, keeping water where it belongs, keeping roads stable. I used to love that moment when a project went from paper to reality. That feeling of, 'I designed this, and it works.' 

But now, I just look at my screen and it's just lines. It's just meaningless lines and numbers, and the responsibility of it is suffocating. I don't care if the bridge holds. I mean, I do care, obviously, I'm not a monster, but I don't *feel* the satisfaction of it. It's just another impossible task on a list of impossible tasks. 

I don't read anymore, I don't watch TV... even just putting on a movie feels like too much of a commitment. I don't want to follow a plot. I don't want to care about characters. I just want to lie on the floor and stare at the baseboards. It's like... you know when you unplug a lamp, and the light just instantly dies? That's what happened to my capacity for pleasure. The cord got pulled, and there's just no current flowing anymore. There's absolutely nothing I look forward to. Nothing.

doctor.intent: Determine the severity of the patient's depression
doctor.question: Do you feel like you're a burden to your loved ones?

target_item.name: Worthlessness_Guilt
target_item.manifestation: I keep telling myself I’m a terrible engineer, a failed wife, and a burden, and I replay every missed calculation or tense email like proof that I ruin things.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I feel like a burden to my loved ones, which directly relates to my feelings of worthlessness and guilt, as I feel like a failed wife and a burden.

patient.answer:
Oh, god, yes. Yes, constantly. I mean, I was just saying how I feel like I'm dragging my husband down into this swamp with me, and that's... that's exactly it. I am a complete burden. I just look at him trying to hold our whole lives together, trying to do the grocery shopping and keep the house running while I'm literally just a useless lump on the floor, and I just keep telling myself what a failed wife I am. I'm completely failing him. 

And it doesn't stop with him, it bleeds into everything. My brain just runs this relentless loop telling me I'm a terrible engineer, too. I'll lie there staring at the wall, and my mind just starts pulling up this... this mental filing cabinet of every mistake I've ever made. I will literally replay every single missed calculation from years ago, or... or I'll obsess over some slightly tense email I sent to a contractor about a grading issue back in 2021. I'll just analyze the wording of this one stupid email over and over, holding it up as like... absolute proof that I ruin things. 

It's like I'm compiling this massive, undeniable dossier of evidence against myself. Proof that I'm incompetent at my job, proof that I'm a drain on my marriage, proof that everything I touch just fails. I just sift through all these past interactions, these tiny little moments that probably nobody else even remembers, and to me, they are just glaring red flags that I am a terrible person and a massive burden to everyone who has the misfortune of relying on me. I just can't stop replaying it all. Every missed decimal point, every awkward conversation... it just plays on a loop to remind me how much I ruin absolutely everything.

doctor.intent: Determine the severity of depressive symptoms
doctor.question: Do you feel like your heavy feeling is getting worse over time?

target_item.name: Depressed_Mood
target_item.manifestation: I came in because I can’t shake this heavy, hopeless feeling, like everything I built after the divorce has collapsed and I’m just sitting under it.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the progression of the 'heavy feeling', which directly refers to my persistent depressed and hopeless mood.

patient.answer:
Worse... I mean, I don't even know if 'worse' really captures it anymore, because that implies there's a bottom to it, you know? But yes... it's just this constant, crushing weight. That’s actually the whole reason I came in, why I finally had to reach out for help. I just... I absolutely cannot shake this heavy, completely hopeless feeling. It just sits on my chest all day and all night. 

It’s like... well, as an engineer, I think about structural integrity a lot, right? After my divorce, I had to completely rebuild my life from the ground up. I had to pour a new foundation, put up new supports, literally reconstruct my entire existence piece by piece just to get back to a place where I was functioning and stable. It took so much work, so much effort to build that new life. And now... it feels like every single thing I built after that divorce has just suffered a catastrophic structural collapse. It all just completely caved in on itself. 

And I’m just... I'm just sitting under it. I'm sitting under all the rubble of my own life, all the concrete and the debris, and it's just pressing down on me. I can't dig myself out. I don't even have the energy to try to move the pieces or assess the damage. I'm just trapped under the weight of it all, and yeah, the longer I sit under it, the heavier and more hopeless it feels.

doctor.intent: Determine the severity of the patient's depression
doctor.question: Do you think your heavy feeling is interfering with your ability to function in daily life?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I was making questionable calls at work and falling apart in meetings, and my supervisor had to take me off active project decisions. At home I stopped keeping up with basic routines and ended up being sent to the emergency department because I didn’t feel safe with my thoughts.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about how my symptoms are interfering with my daily life and ability to function, which directly corresponds to the functional impairment item.

patient.answer:
Interfering... yeah. Yeah, it’s completely derailed everything. I mean, I was telling you earlier about how much I used to care about my job and the infrastructure and the calculations, right? Well, it got to the point where I was actually making really questionable calls at work. Like, I was reviewing a grading plan for this new commercial development, and I just... I couldn't process the elevation data anymore. I was signing off on things that just didn't make logical sense, just staring at the screen and guessing because my brain was so bogged down in that swamp. 

And then in meetings... oh god, the meetings. We have these weekly coordination meetings with the architects and city planners, and I would just sit there and completely fall apart. I'd start crying over a minor timeline adjustment, or I'd just freeze up, completely blank, and not be able to answer basic questions about soil compaction that I've known the answers to for ten years. It was so humiliating. Finally, my supervisor had to pull me into his office and officially take me off all active project decisions. He had to physically remove my authority because I was messing up so badly and he could see I was just crumbling in real time. 

And then at home... I know I mentioned the Sunday breakfasts earlier, but it goes so far beyond just not cooking. I completely stopped keeping up with basic routines. Any routine, really. I'm talking about going four or five days without showering, wearing the same sweatpants until they literally smell, letting the mail pile up on the counter until it falls onto the floor and I just step over it... I couldn't even brush my teeth. The effort required to just lift a toothbrush to my mouth felt like trying to lift a steel I-beam. 

And it just... it kept piling up, the inability to do anything, until it got so dark. The weight of all that rubble I was talking about, it just crushed me to the point where I actually ended up being sent to the emergency department. My husband had to take me in because... well, because I just didn't feel safe with my own thoughts anymore. The things my brain was telling me to do just to escape that heavy feeling, to escape being such a massive burden on him and everyone else... I was terrified of myself. I couldn't be trusted alone in my own house. So, yes. It's not just interfering. It has completely dismantled my ability to function in every possible way.

I know I just said this, but yes, it really is. It’s... I mean, it’s the whole reason I’m here, the whole reason I finally made the appointment. I just... I can't shake it. This heavy, completely hopeless feeling. It’s just getting heavier and heavier, and it's like I was telling you before, about how I had to rebuild my entire life after my divorce. I put so much work into pouring that new foundation, making sure everything was structurally sound, making sure I was stable and functioning. And now... now it feels like all of that, everything I built, has just suffered this catastrophic collapse. 

It's all just caved in, and I'm just... I'm just sitting under it. All the rubble, all the concrete, all the pieces of the life I tried to put back together. It’s all just pressing down on me, and I can’t move. I can’t dig myself out. And the longer I sit under it, the heavier it gets, and the more hopeless I feel. doctor.intent: Determine the severity of the patient's depression
doctor.question: Do you think you might be at risk of harming yourself today?

target_item.name: Death_Suicide
target_item.manifestation: I’ve been thinking that it would be easier if I didn’t wake up, and the thoughts got intense enough that I scared myself and called the employee assistance program.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I am at risk of harming myself today, which directly assesses suicidal ideation and risk of suicide.

patient.answer:
Today... I mean, today is really just a continuation of this whole nightmare, right? But... yes. I think so. Or, I'm trying not to be, but... I've been having these thoughts. 

At first, it was just this passive, quiet sort of wish when I would go to bed. I would just lie there in the dark, staring at the ceiling, and I’d think about how much easier it would be if I just... didn’t wake up. If I could just stay asleep and not have to open my eyes and face the crushing weight of all that rubble again. Just let the collapse be final, you know? It just seemed like the most logical, peaceful solution to stop the pain.

But then... recently, it stopped being just a quiet wish. The thoughts started getting so incredibly loud and intense, just looping in my head over and over like a stress-test simulation that won't shut off. It got to the point where I actually scared myself. I mean, genuinely terrified myself, because I realized I wasn't just wishing for it anymore, I was feeling actively pulled toward it. I was sitting in my living room, and the urge was so heavy... that’s actually what prompted me to reach out. I panicked and ended up calling the Employee Assistance Program through my firm. I just dug through my wallet and dialed the number on the back of my benefits card because I knew if I didn't connect with someone right that very second, I couldn't guarantee what I would do. 

So... yeah. The risk is there. I'm fighting it, but the thoughts are just so loud.
